notes.claim: A live-tracking method clamps a probe on each feeder to measure its earth leakage current without interrupting distribution.
An insulation fault locator sends a test current pulse through the live conductors, the fault and the earth wire, and clamps on each circuit detect it.
To find a fault, engineers isolate circuits one at a time, with essential services covered, until the reading recovers.
Insulation measurement is the test of insulation resistance in the switched-off, de-energised system.

A clamp on each feeder at supply frequency is not reliable on a network with many feeders, some highly capacitive, because a short faulty feeder's earth current is hard to tell from a long capacitive feeder's.
Fault tracking uses a low-frequency signal so the network's leakage capacitance does not disturb it, though not below 2.5 Hz, where a magnetic sensor struggles to detect it.
Shutting down distributions one by one is hard at sea: not every system can be switched off, and the fault can disappear because the faulty load has already switched off.
An insulation monitor cannot measure insulation faults in loads that are switched off.
The locator's test current is seen by every measuring current transformer on the faulty circuit's path.
The locator limits its test current to a maximum value.
A portable locating set injects a locating current of 1 to 25 mA and reads it with clamps.
Each fault-location sensor is a toroidal current transformer around all the conductors of its circuit.
Insulation measurement (a dead test) and insulation monitoring (live) are easily mixed up.
Equipment likely to influence an insulation resistance test, or be damaged by it, is disconnected before the test.
An insulation monitor's maker says to disconnect the monitor before checking insulation.
Ship rules measure a switchboard's insulation resistance at a DC voltage of at least 500 V.
Common causes of earth faults on ships are water in junction boxes and deck lights, damaged cables, and insulation breaking down in motors and heaters.
